reagent

/ree-AY-jent/ - 're' plus 'agent' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A reagent is a substance added to take part in a chemical reaction — combined, changed, or used up as the reaction runs, most often to test what a sample contains.

One drop of the iodine reagent turned the potato slice blue-black, betraying the starch hidden inside.

Example

The stream-monitoring volunteers unpacked a rack of small bottles at each bend of the creek, one reagent for every question they meant to put to the water. A few drops of the first in a vial of creek water blushed pink: nitrates. The second went cloudy: phosphates, likely washed down from a fertilized lawn upstream. By the fourth test the team had a chemical portrait of the river, drawn one reagent at a time.

Reagent is the precise word for those bottled chemicals, because a reagent is a substance added to take part in a chemical reaction — combined, changed, or used up as it runs — most often to make a sample reveal what it contains. The creek water answered no questions on its own; each reagent went in, reacted or refused to, and the color did the reporting. An ingredient merely belongs to a mixture; a reagent is sent in with a job to do.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

catalyst: A catalyst speeds a reaction up but comes out unchanged on the other side, ready to work again. A reagent is a working participant: it gets used up, combined, or transformed by the reaction it drives.

indicator: An indicator is the narrow specialist — a substance whose whole job is to signal, usually by a color change, that something is present. Reagent is the broader working word for any substance added to take part in a reaction, whether it signals, dissolves, or builds.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

product: what the reaction yields at the end — a reagent goes in, a product comes out

filler: an inactive substance added only for bulk, with no reaction asked of it

Where it sits · how hard the substance pushes the reaction

ingredient → reagent → accelerant

ingredient vs. reagent: Ingredient is weaker than reagent — an ingredient only has to be present in the mix, while a reagent is added precisely so that a chemical reaction will happen.

accelerant vs. reagent: Accelerant goes further than reagent — a reagent starts or steers a reaction at a working pace, while an accelerant whips one into racing, often destructive speed.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-: back, in response

Root — ag: to do, to drive, to act (Latin agere)

Suffix — -ent: a thing that does

Put it together: Re- (back, in response) + ag (to do, to drive — Latin agere) + -ent (a thing that does) = 'something that acts back.' Take off the prefix and agent appears, Latin's doer — and a reagent is the doer you add to the flask: it meets the sample and reacts. The same tireless root built act, agenda, and agency, English's whole vocabulary of getting things done.

Use the root in a new word: agency: Historians still argue over how much agency the villagers had in the reforms that carried their name.

Root Check

Word Choice

technical / matter-of-fact

Reagent is bench vocabulary: use it for a substance added to make a chemical reaction go, especially in a test. A kitchen has ingredients; a lab has reagents — swap the two words in either direction and the sentence sounds wrong. Keep the working family straight: a catalyst speeds the reaction but comes out unchanged, an indicator only signals, and the reagent is the participant that gets used up doing the job. And this unit's prefix is hiding in plain sight: a reagent is literally a re-agent, the agent you add so the sample will act back.
